clue.text: Presumably it wouldn't appeal to the big-game hunter

definitions.text: Presumably it wouldn't appeal to the big-game hunter

parts.words: Presumably it wouldn't appeal to the big-game hunter
parts.note: the clue pictures a hunter of lions and elephants, but read the other way it is a game played on a small table, a mere trifle of a game, that would hold no charm for someone after big game

explanation.surface: A safari hunter would surely turn up his nose at this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big-game' sends you to the savannah; the answer is both a small indoor board game (balls struck into numbered holes) and a word for a trifle, the opposite of anything big.
explanation.definitionFit: A bagatelle is a table game and also a trifle, so it is the small game that a seeker of big game ignores.

clue.text: A mouthful of sea-water ?

definitions.text: A mouthful of sea-water ?

parts.words: A mouthful of sea-water
parts.note: a 'mouthful' suggests a bite or gulp, but it is the sea's mouth, a wide bay, and the word sounds like a bite

explanation.surface: A gulp of salty water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouthful' suggests a gulp; the answer is a curving bay, like a mouth of sea, and sounds like 'bite'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide curving bay in a coastline is a mouth-shaped inlet of sea.

clue.text: Presumably he had a consuming interest in pilgrims!

definitions.text: Presumably he had a consuming interest in pilgrims!

parts.words: Presumably he had a consuming interest in pilgrims
parts.note: Rabelais's giant once ate six pilgrims in a salad, so his 'interest' in them was literally consuming

explanation.surface: A man deeply fascinated by religious travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Rabelais's book, the giant swallows six pilgrims hidden among the lettuces of his salad; 'consuming' means eating, not absorbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabelais's giant ate pilgrims in his salad, so he took a consuming interest in them.

clue.text: There are no —— in plain and simple faith " (6). (J. Caesar).

definitions.text: There are no —— in plain and simple faith " (6). (J. Caesar).

parts.words: There are no —— in plain and simple faith
parts.note: Brutus in Julius Caesar, Act 4: 'There are no' deceits 'in plain and simple faith'; the blank asks for the missing word

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Brutus quarrels with Cassius and says honest faith uses no deceits; the missing word completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Deceits and ruses have no place in honest faith, as Brutus says.

clue.text: To be found in Billingsgate

definitions.text: To be found in Billingsgate

indicators.note: the answer's letters can be found inside the market's name, signalling a run of consecutive letters

parts.words: Billingsgate

explanation.surface: Something you would come across at the London fish market.
explanation.walkthrough: BILLINGSGATE was London's fish market, and a ling (a fish of the cod family) is sold there; its letters also sit inside the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A cod-like sea fish is exactly what a London fish market would stock.

clue.text: " Yes, Heaven is — at home, The big blue cap that always fits " (Chesterton).

definitions.text: " Yes, Heaven is — at home, The big blue cap that always fits " (Chesterton).

parts.words: Yes, Heaven is — at home, The big blue cap that always fits
parts.note: G. K. Chesterton's lines say the sky is at home in every place, a big blue cap that fits all heads; the blank asks for the missing word

explanation.surface: A Chesterton quotation about the sky with one word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterton pictures the sky as a cap that fits any head, so heaven is at home in all places; the missing word completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: The sky covers all places alike, so heaven is at home in all of them.

clue.text: Not craved by a merryman

definitions.text: Not craved by a merryman

parts.words: Not craved by a merryman
parts.note: quotes Jack Point's song 'I have a song to sing, O!' in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Yeomen of the Guard: the moping merryman 'sipped no sup and craved no' morsel

explanation.surface: Something a jolly fellow has no appetite for.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue completes a line of Gilbert and Sullivan: 'Who sipped no sup, and who craved no crumb, As he sighed for the love of a ladye.'
explanation.definitionFit: The sad jester of the song lost his appetite, wanting not even the smallest morsel of bread.

clue.text: Game fellows, but there's really no life in them

definitions.text: Game fellows, but there's really no life in them

parts.words: Game fellows, but there's really no life in them
parts.note: 'game fellows' sounds like plucky men, but these are the 'men' of a board game, carved pieces with no life at all

explanation.surface: Plucky chaps who are nonetheless dull company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like 'brave'; the 'fellows' are the pieces on a chessboard: king, queen, knights and pawns, all inanimate.
explanation.definitionFit: The pieces of the board game are called men, yet they are carved wood with no life.

clue.text: It's the custom for us to be on time

definitions.text: custom

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits on top of the other, so this phrase places the first word above the second

parts.words: us
time
parts.note: an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Being punctual is our habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be on time' reads as punctuality, but 'on' is positional: in a down entry one piece sits on top of the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Established practice or habitual way of doing things is a custom.

clue.text: Where tongues wag under canvas ?

definitions.text: Where tongues wag under canvas ?

parts.words: Where tongues wag under canvas
parts.note: 'tongues wag' suggests gossip in a camp, but it is the clappers of a bell, and the answer is a conical tent shaped like one

explanation.surface: Gossip around the campsite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongues wag' means gossip; a bell's tongue is its clapper, and these round, pole-centred tents are named for their bell shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Conical canvas shelters shaped like a bell, used by armies and campers, are named after the bell's shape.

clue.text: Adoring can be an intricate business

definitions.text: an intricate business
definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase; the answer is the adjective from the Gordian knot, standing for any hopelessly tangled affair

indicators.note: the letters of the first word can be made into another word when rearranged, so this phrase signals the reshuffle

parts.words: Adoring

explanation.surface: Being devoted to someone can get complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' tells you ADORING can be rearranged into the answer. The Gordian knot, tied by King Gordius and cut by Alexander, is the byword for something intricate.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordian describes a tangled problem, after the famously complex knot of Gordium.

clue.text: Sphere of vision ?

definitions.text: Sphere of vision ?

parts.words: Sphere of vision
parts.note: 'sphere' suggests a field or range of sight, but here it is a literal ball: the round organ we see with

explanation.surface: The range of what one can see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sphere of vision' reads like 'field of view'; take 'sphere' literally as a globe and it is the organ of sight itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ of sight is a round globe in the socket, so it is literally the globe that sees.

clue.text: Beggar that I am, I am even poor in (Hamlet)

definitions.text: Beggar that I am, I am even poor in

parts.words: Beggar that I am, I am even poor in
parts.note: Hamlet's words to Rosencrantz and Guildenstern in Act 2: 'Beggar that I am, I am even poor in' gratitude; the blank asks for the missing word

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet with its last word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet greets his old schoolfellows and says he is too poor even in gratitude to repay their visit; the missing word completes the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Expressions of gratitude are what Hamlet says he is too poor to give his visitors.

clue.text: Order to assume a sinister look ?

definitions.text: Order to assume a sinister look ?

parts.words: Order to assume a sinister look
parts.note: 'sinister' is Latin for left-hand, so a 'sinister look' is a glance to the left, as commanded on parade

explanation.surface: A command to put on a menacing expression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinister' looks like 'menacing', but in heraldry and Latin it means left; the clue is the drill-ground order to turn the head to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: On parade, this command makes soldiers turn their heads to the left, sinister being the heraldic word for left.

clue.text: Are they made to the railway cloak room?

definitions.text: Are they made to the railway cloak room?

parts.words: Are they made to the railway cloak room
parts.note: the clue imagines visits to the left-luggage office to collect a trunk

explanation.surface: A question about trips to the station's luggage office.
explanation.walkthrough: Long-distance phone calls in Britain were called trunk calls; the clue pictures calls on the luggage office, where trunks are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-distance phone calls were known as trunk calls, and a trunk is luggage left at the station.

clue.text: There be land ones, said Shylock

definitions.text: There be land ones, said Shylock

parts.words: There be land ones, said Shylock
parts.note: Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, Act 1, speaks of 'land-... and water-..., land-thieves and water-thieves', meaning robbers and pirates

explanation.surface: A line attributed to Shakespeare's moneylender.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock weighs the risks to Antonio's ships: 'there be land-rats and water-rats'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock uses these rodents as a figure for thieves ashore and at sea, contrasting land ones with water ones.

clue.text: His is presumably a war-time calling

definitions.text: His is presumably a war-time calling

parts.words: His is presumably a war-time calling
parts.note: a soldier held in reserve is called up only when war comes, so his 'calling' is a summons in wartime

explanation.surface: A man whose vocation suits a time of war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like 'vocation'; it is the call-up of a soldier kept in reserve, made only in wartime.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the reserve forces is called up to serve only when war breaks out.

clue.text: "'The Bishop's eye "

definitions.text: "'The Bishop's eye "

parts.words: The Bishop's eye
parts.note: the cleric who oversees a part of a diocese for its bishop has long been called 'oculus episcopi', the bishop's eye

explanation.surface: A phrase for the one who watches over a diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: The traditional title 'oculus episcopi' (the bishop's eye) was given to the senior cleric who inspects parishes on the bishop's behalf.
explanation.definitionFit: This senior cleric oversees parishes for the bishop, so he is called the bishop's eye in church tradition.

clue.text: The Mecca of bargain hunters in London ?

definitions.text: The Mecca of bargain hunters in London ?

parts.words: The Mecca of bargain hunters in London
parts.note: a City of London street whose name comes from Old English 'ceap', a market, reads as the side where things are inexpensive

explanation.surface: Where London's thrifty shoppers flock.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheapside is a street in the City of London, once its main market; its name reads as the inexpensive side.
explanation.definitionFit: This City street was London's old market, and its name suggests the inexpensive side of town.

clue.text: Wherefrom high-pitched voices might be heard ?

definitions.text: Wherefrom high-pitched voices might be heard ?

parts.words: Wherefrom high-pitched voices might be heard
parts.note: 'high-pitched' suggests shrill voices, but here they are pitched high up, the muezzin calling from tall mosque towers

explanation.surface: A source of shrill sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-pitched' suggests shrill tones; the voices are high because the muezzin calls to prayer from a mosque's tall slender tower.
explanation.definitionFit: The muezzin calls to prayer from these tall mosque towers, so voices come from high up.

clue.text: Still capable of creating a Tory '. saint

definitions.text: Still

indicators.note: the following words are able to make the answer once their letters are rearranged, which signals the anagram

parts.words: a
Tory
parts.note: taken as written

parts.words: saint
parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Unmoving, yet able to produce a Conservative saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capable of creating' says the letters of A TORY SAINT can be rearranged to make the answer. 'Still' looks like 'nevertheless' but is the adjective meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Something motionless stays where it is, not moving at all.

clue.text: They go to war for protection

definitions.text: They go to war for protection

parts.words: They go to war for protection
parts.note: read literally, these four letters go after the word war to make the wartime protectors of the air-raid patrols, the ...

explanation.surface: Soldiers who fight to keep others safe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests soldiers; instead the letters attach to WAR to make WARDENS, the civil defence protectors of the 1940s. The answer is also a lair, a refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: Lairs are animals' refuges, and joined to war the letters make wardens, wartime protectors.

clue.text: Not so well off in purdah ?

definitions.text: Not so well off

indicators.note: the answer's letters are all in the last word, rearranged, so this little word points to the anagram here

parts.words: purdah

explanation.surface: A woman in seclusion who has fallen on hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of PURDAH (the seclusion of women in parts of South Asia) are rearranged; 'in' says the answer lies within that word reshuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Being short of money means one is poorly off, lacking funds.

clue.text: Occupation for those gifted with second sight ?

definitions.text: Occupation for those gifted with second sight ?

parts.words: Occupation for those gifted with second sight
parts.note: 'second sight' suggests clairvoyance, but here it means looking again, a ..., which is the scholar's careful work

explanation.surface: A career suited to clairvoyants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second sight' looks like psychic power; the answer splits as RE-SEARCH, a second look, the job of the investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholarly investigation means looking again and again, a second search, so it suits those with a second look.

clue.text: Bill for housebreaking

definitions.text: Bill for housebreaking

parts.words: Bill for housebreaking
parts.note: 'Bill' looks like an invoice, but it is the first name of the burglar in Dickens's Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: An invoice for a burglary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' suggests a charge or a law; it is Bill Sikes, the violent housebreaker of Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Bill Sikes is the brutal burglar of Oliver Twist.

clue.text: It's plain a legislator's in step.

definitions.text: plain
definitions.note: the definition is singular, while the answer names the South American grasslands, used of one great plain

indicators.note: the article and the lawmaker are placed inside the dance step, so 'in' signals the container

parts.words: step
parts.note: pas is the French word for a step, used in ballet

parts.words: a
legislator's
parts.note: MP, a Member of Parliament, is a legislator; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A lawmaker keeps in time with a flat stretch of land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'step' looks like part of the surface's marching image, but it is the ballet term from French. 'It's' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The grassy treeless lowlands of Argentina form a vast flat expanse of grassland.

clue.text: Polish settlement by the Thames?

definitions.text: Polish
definitions.meaning: a gloss or shine on a surface

definitions.text: settlement by the Thames?
definitions.meaning: a district near Richmond on the River Thames in south-west London

explanation.surface: A Polish community living beside London's river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like the nationality; it is the noun meaning shine. The other sense is a place near Richmond on the River Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A shine on a surface is a gloss, and the name is also that of a riverside district near Richmond.

clue.text: Aeroplanes, that would be thrown overboard before morning

definitions.text: Aeroplanes

parts.words: that would be thrown overboard before morning
parts.note: place AM, morning, after these letters and they spell ..., cargo thrown overboard from a ship

explanation.surface: Aircraft that ought to be dumped into the sea by dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer before AM (morning) and it becomes JETSAM, goods thrown overboard to lighten a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Jet-powered aircraft are commonly called by the name of their engines.

clue.text: Where pen-pals might go for a dip ?

definitions.text: Where pen-pals might go for a dip ?

parts.words: Where pen-pals might go for a dip
parts.note: 'pen-pals' are taken as fountain pens and nibs, and their 'dip' is the plunge into the ink pot on the desk

explanation.surface: A bathing spot for people who exchange letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen-pals' suggests letter-writing friends and 'dip' a swim; the pens themselves dip into the desk's ink-holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk's ink pot is where an old-fashioned pen is dipped to be recharged.

clue.text: Conclusively discreet?

definitions.text: Conclusively discreet?

parts.words: Conclusively discreet
parts.note: split the answer's sense: 'conclusively' gives a conclusion, an end, and 'discreet' gives wise, so the clue reads the word as end plus prudent

explanation.surface: Prudent in a decisive way.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer means end-on or lengthways, but the clue reads it as two words: END ('conclusively') and WISE ('discreet').
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means with the end foremost; read in two parts it is a conclusion followed by a prudent word.

clue.text: One of these jobs was Cowper's

definitions.text: One of these jobs was Cowper's

parts.words: One of these jobs was Cowper's
parts.note: the poet William Cowper titled his long blank-verse poem of 1785 after a single assigned job, so one such piece of work belonged to him

explanation.surface: A piece of work once given to a man named Cowper.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper, the 18th-century English poet, is known for a long poem whose title is the singular of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces of assigned work are jobs; Cowper's best-known poem is titled after one.

clue.text: Such uphill work is never' done

definitions.text: Such uphill work is never' done

parts.words: Such uphill work is never' done
parts.note: in Greek myth a king was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever, only for it to roll back each time

explanation.surface: Climbing labour that never finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Sisyphus, punished in Hades, pushes a rock up a slope endlessly; his name describes any endless, futile toil.
explanation.definitionFit: Endless, futile labour is named after the Greek king doomed to push a boulder uphill forever.
